newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Iraq, Middle East, Bosnia on EU meeting agenda.
newsitem.headline: Iraq, Middle East, Bosnia on EU meeting agenda.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers sought agreement on Saturday on a range of issues from the Middle East to Bosnia, but were deeply divided over U.S. attacks on Iraq.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, host of an informal meeting in southwest Ireland, said his colleagues believed a high-level EU delegation to Israel should meet the Palestine Liberation Organisation in disputed East Jerusalem.
"It is important that we keep a balance in our relations with the Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority," he said.
The meeting was due to discuss what role the EU could take to further the Middle East Peace process.

The ministers also planned to use their two-day informal retreat in the town of Tralee to discuss a response to U.S. trade laws concerning Cuba, Iran and Libya that are widely opposed outside the United States.

But the failure of the bloc to agree a common position on America's attack on Iraq -- with Britain and Germany backing the move and France, Spain and Italy withholding support -- was set to cause some discomfort at the meeting.
"It's a very damaging situation because it puts us (the EU) on the margins," Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos told reporters as the meeting began.

Britain, Washington's closest European ally, earlier in the week tried to get the bloc to issue a strong statement of support for the U.S. attack, launched in response to an Iraqi incursion into the Kurdish "safe haven" in northern Iraq.
But France, believing the attack to be an inappropriate reaction, blocked the move.
Ministers arriving on Saturday accepted that there were sharp differences, but emphasised that the bloc was united in its opposition to Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein's actions.
"The point of agreement is greater than the differences," British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind told reporters.
Speaking to BBC radio earlier, Rifkind had called on his colleagues to support the United States or come up with a better strategy against Saddam.
EU sources said the differences in the bloc were too great to come up with a meaningful joint position, but predicted the leaders would find a way of papering over their split.
The ministers were also due to be briefed by Carl Bildt, the international community's Bosnia monitor, on the state of the divided country as it prepared for elections on September 14.

Belgian Foreign Minister Erik Derycke was due to call for more international and EU cooperation in combating child sexual abuse, following the recent uncovering of a paedophile ring and the murders of abducted children in Belgium.

Irish officials said they expected the session to endorse October 5 as the date of an informal one-day summit in Dublin to review the bloc's future and the status of a review of its founding treaties.

Ireland will host another summit in December but the October heads of state session was requested to deal with matters shelved while the bloc was paralysed by a dispute over Mad Cow disease and British objections to a ban on its beef exports.
On Sunday, the ministers were to discuss the state of progress in the bloc's negotiations on a new treaty, known as the inter-governmental conference (IGC).
Many countries believe the talks are moving too slowly. "We still have a lot of homework to do," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told Reuters.
